story.title: Janaka’s feeding test and the poor couple’s devotional gift
story.completeness_basis: All bodies and named transitions in this bounded witness-local scope are read and extracted; its stated ending is present.

event.details: Kauṇḍinya recounts Nārada visiting Gaṇeśa after many days. The sage bows, praises the fruitful sight and stands with joined hands. Gaṇeśa holds his hand and seats him. Nārada says he came to report an astonishing matter and would depart after bowing. Gaṇeśa asks him to describe everything before returning to his hermitage.
event.outcome: Nārada receives an explicit invitation to tell the report.

event.details: Nārada reports Janaka of Mithilā as proud, generous and learned in Vedas and Vedāṅgas: he continually feeds and honours Brahmins with ornaments, clothing and gifts, gives wealth to poor, blind and destitute people, and grants petitions. Nārada wonders whether Gaṇeśa’s satisfaction accounts for undiminished wealth. On visiting, Janaka mocks him through pride in Brahman knowledge. Nārada praises Gaṇeśa as giver of the king’s devotional desires, but Janaka claims to be lord, giver, enjoyer, protector, maker, cause and instrument, with none other in three worlds. Angered, Nārada says God alone makes the world, challenges the king’s apparent religious display, and promises evidence soon.
event.outcome: The king’s attributed claims and Nārada’s challenge motivate the later test.

event.details: Having heard the report, Gaṇeśa honours Nārada with arghya, ornaments, flowers and sandal. With permission Nārada goes to Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha. Gaṇeśa comes to Mithilā to test the king’s devotion, wearing a repulsive old Brahmin form with bleeding wounds, flies and missing teeth. He stumbles, faints and falls amid children; people cover their noses and spit. At the royal gate he asks to be announced as an old, hungry Brahmin guest desiring a meal. Janaka orders his admission, observes his filthy clothes, trembling, bleeding and exhaustion, suspects a divine test, and resolves to satisfy him if merit allows.
event.outcome: The narrator identifies the disguised deity; Janaka separately conjectures a divine guest.

event.details: The guest says he came after hearing Janaka’s fame and asks food until fully satisfied, promising the merit of one hundred sacrifices. Janaka takes him inside, honours him and serves tasty food. The guest consumes the entire portion in one mouthful, then a mountain-sized portion in one mouthful, then prepared food sufficient for ten thousand. Rice is put to cook in innumerable vessels and he eats every finished batch.
event.outcome: Successive immense servings fail to satisfy the guest.

event.details: Some advisers conjecture that the guest is a Rākṣasa and gifts to such beings give no merit; others say even the three worlds could not satisfy him and urge offering grain. All palace, city and village grain is gathered and consumed, still without satisfaction. Messengers report none remains; Janaka lowers his head. The guest departs house to house asking food. Residents explain their grain was collected by the king and already eaten by him. He questions how he can leave unsatisfied after hearing Janaka’s unparalleled giving fame. Amid silence he finds the Brahmin home of Virocanā and Triśiras, enters like its owner, and sees no equipment or metal vessels.
event.outcome: Janaka’s resources are exhausted; the test continues in a poor couple’s home.

event.details: The couple sits on bare earth, with sky as covering, avoiding contact with metals. They eat unasked food, use water for their rites and maintain purity. Amid flies and mosquitoes their Gaṇeśa image is worshipped with flowers and leaves in exclusive devotion. The disguised guest says Janaka did not satisfy him and ostentatious action cannot preserve sattva; he asks anything in their house that could satisfy him. The couple wonders how they, poor people, can feed one whom an emperor could not, comparing a drop with rivers unable to fill the ocean. He says even a small devotional gift greatly satisfies him; abundant gifts without devotion or given for display are fruitless.
event.outcome: The guest explains why devotional giving differs from abundance without devotion.

event.details: The couple swears nothing remains except one dūrvā sprout left from the morning Gaṇeśa worship. At the guest’s request Virocanā offers that single sprout with devotion, imagining rice, pāyasa, varied cooked dishes, accompaniments and lickable or suckable foods upon it. He joyfully eats it; his stomach-fire immediately subsides, he gains complete satisfaction and embraces Triśiras.
event.outcome: One actually offered sprout accompanied by imagined foods satisfies the guest whom abundant actual food did not satisfy.

event.details: Gaṇeśa abandons the repulsive disguise and appears four-armed, lotus-eyed and trunk-bearing, holding lotus, axe, rosary and tusk, wearing costly crown, earrings, divine clothing and scents. He invites the couple to choose their desired boon. They ask for firm devotion wherever they are born, or liberation from the difficult ocean of transmigration, wanting nothing else. He assents with tathā, joyfully embraces Triśiras again and vanishes.
event.outcome: The deity explicitly assents and withdraws; no later death or selected alternative is invented.

event.details: Kauṇḍinya tells Aśrayā that this is why he offers dūrvā: the deity who remained unsatisfied by innumerable foods gained full satisfaction through one sprout. He states that hearing the offering’s greatness gives all wishes; devoted hearing or telling brings sons, wealth and enjoyment here and hereafter, Gaṇeśa devotion, and liberation for a desireless person.
event.outcome: Kauṇḍinya applies the completed test account to his own practice.
